children: By Khadeeja Safdar and Joe Palazzolo

Federal authorities have opened a probe into Darren Indyke and Richard Kahn, Jeffrey Epstein's longtime lawyer and accountant who are now his estate executors, according to people familiar with the matter.

Federal prosecutors in Manhattan in recent months have been scheduling interviews with potential witnesses and have requested documents about their dealings with Indyke, Epstein's lawyer, and Kahn, his accountant, the people said. The documents include emails and financial records.

The two men have previously said they didn't know Epstein was engaged in sex trafficking and denied being complicit in or knowingly facilitating any crimes. They said none of the women ever reported to them they were being sexually abused. A lawyer for Kahn referred to the prior statement, and a lawyer for Indyke didn't respond.

"We don't comment on the existence, or lack thereof, of investigations," a Justice Department spokeswoman said. "We have always said with regard to Epstein that if the evidence presents itself, we will investigate."

The Justice Department released millions of the Epstein case files earlier this year, revealing the sex offender's private correspondence with business leaders, politicians, academics and many of his victims. The disclosure prompted arrests of some officials in Europe, corporate resignations and congressional hearings.

Justice Department officials have previously said they didn't find evidence to charge anyone beyond Ghislaine Maxwell in connection with Epstein's activities. In a congressional hearing after the FBI files release, then-attorney general Pam Bondi stated that the Federal Bureau of Investigation was waiting to hear from victims or anyone with relevant information.

The Wall Street Journal couldn't determine what charges are being explored. People interviewed by prosecutors described Kahn's and Indyke's roles in legal entities that allegedly helped conceal Epstein's activities and the two men's handling of financial and legal matters involving young women, according to people familiar with the interviews.

The Journal published an investigation last year reporting that the two men were officers of Epstein entities that obscured transactions, arranged cash for Epstein, made payments to women and facilitated Epstein's immigration schemes. In statements, the two men denied wrongdoing.
Neither man was questioned about their work for Epstein in 2019 and 2020 when federal prosecutors in Manhattan were investigating Epstein and Maxwell on sex-trafficking charges, the Journal reported.

Both men were hired before Epstein pleaded guilty in Florida and stayed on with him until the very end. After Epstein's death in 2019, Indyke and Kahn were left to manage his estate and settle lawsuits brought by Epstein's victims. The estate set up a compensation fund that has paid more than $120 million to dozens of eligible victims and has resolved other claims outside the program.

The men are among the top beneficiaries of a trust that was to collect Epstein's remaining assets after all claims against the estate are resolved. Indyke could receive $50 million and Kahn could get $25 million from the Epstein estate, according to documents.

Earlier this year, the House Oversight Committee issued a subpoena to request both men answer questions under oath. The committee has been investigating the government's handling of the Epstein case and has questioned some of Epstein's powerful associates, including former President Bill Clinton, Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates and billionaire Leon Black. They all said they were unaware of Epstein's criminal activities.

The House recently voted to hold Black in contempt of Congress. The former Apollo Global Management leader has sued the committee, saying it overstepped its authority in seeking certain nondisclosure agreements.
